competing_hypotheses: With a further grid refinement to nx=320 (h≈0.625 mm at crack tip), the changes in total strain energy and remote crack opening displacement will be below 0.2%, indicating mesh convergence; therefore the current mesh (or the pattern) is sufficient for linear elastic fracture assessment, and no further mesh refinement is needed.

Even after refining to nx=320, the relative changes in strain energy or opening displacement will exceed 0.2%, or the peak stress will still be rising significantly, casting doubt on the reliability of the global quantities for fracture evaluation; additional refinement or a different meshing strategy (such as introducing crack-tip singular elements) would be required.
evidence_refs: From h=2.5 mm (nx=80) to h=1.25 mm (nx=160), the relative change in strain energy was 0.20% and in opening displacement 0.24%, both below 0.5% but not below 0.2%.

Peak stress σ_y continues to increase (from 289 MPa to 402 MPa) as expected for a linear-elastic crack tip singularity, indicating that local stress convergence is not achievable but global energy and displacement are converging.
Energy balance remains close to machine zero in all runs, confirming solution accuracy.
uncertainties: No fracture mechanics quantity (stress intensity factor, J-integral) has been directly computed or compared against an analytical reference.
The choice of 0.2% tolerance for strain energy and opening displacement is heuristic and may not guarantee sufficiently accurate K_I or G predictions.
The crack-tip mesh still lacks a built-in singularity; a very fine mesh may artificially limit the peak stress but still fail to capture the exact stress field near the tip.

The execution environment appears only able to uniformly refine the global mesh (via nx) rather than introduce local topological changes; this may lead to excessive element counts and computational cost without guaranteeing convergence at the crack tip.

experiment.purpose: Test whether a further uniform mesh refinement to nx=320 (yielding h≈0.625 mm at the crack tip) produces changes in global strain energy and opening displacement below 0.2%, thereby deciding if the mesh can be accepted for linear-elastic fracture evaluation.
experiment.change: Increase the global mesh parameter nx from 160 to 320 while keeping the same structured refinement pattern (so that the crack-tip element size is halved to approximately 0.625 mm).
hold_fixed: Plate outer dimensions (200 mm × 200 mm) and thickness (10 mm)
Material properties (Young’s modulus 210000 MPa, Poisson’s ratio 0.3)
Uniform tensile loading of 100 MPa on top and bottom edges
Analysis type (2D plane stress linear elastic)
Mesh design strategy (structured grid with local refinement at crack tip; only the minimum element size is altered)
experiment.decision_rule: Compute the relative change in strain energy and in remote opening displacement between the current nx=160 (h=1.25 mm) and the new nx=320 (h=0.625 mm) results. If both relative changes are ≤ 0.2%, accept the mesh as converged and suitable for fracture assessment (i.e., stop refining). Otherwise, flag the mesh as potentially insufficient, and recommend either a still finer refinement (e.g., nx=640) or an alternative approach (e.g., fracture-mechanics specific output).
experiment.stop_condition: The experiment is complete once the analysis with nx=320 is finished and the relative changes are calculated.
